profile.name: Indian dance
profile.tagline: Ancient performance traditions classified into classical, folk, and tribal styles.
profile.insight: Rooted in the ancient Sanskrit text Natya Shastra, Indian classical dances enact complex mythological stories almost exclusively through hand gestures and facial expressions.
profile.profile: Indian dance encompasses numerous styles classified generally as classical, folk, or tribal. Originating across different regions, these traditions are deeply rooted in Hindu mythology and ancient texts like the Natya Shastra. The Sangeet Natak Akademi currently recognizes eight classical forms, each maintaining unique regional aesthetics, costumes, and movement vocabularies. Folk and tribal dances, by contrast, serve as oral traditions expressing the daily work, rituals, and local customs of village communities.
profile.profile_long:
Dance in India comprises numerous styles of dances, generally classified as classical, folk, or tribal. Different forms originated in distinct parts of the country, developing according to local traditions and absorbing elements from other regions. The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognizes eight traditional dances as Indian classical dances: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, and Sattriya. These classical forms share roots in the Sanskrit text Natya Shastra and the religious performance arts of Hinduism, historically taught through a guru-shishya parampara (teacher-disciple tradition).

The origins of dance in India extend back to ancient times, evidenced by paleolithic and neolithic cave paintings at the UNESCO world heritage site of Bhimbetka rock shelters in Madhya Pradesh. Archaeological finds from the Indus Valley Civilisation, such as the 10.5-centimetre bronze Dancing Girl figurine dated to about 2500 BCE, further illustrate early dance postures. Vedic texts integrate rituals with dramatic performance arts and dialogues discussing spiritual themes. The foundational surviving classical text, the Natya Shastra, is attributed to the sage Bharata and structured into 36 chapters detailing gesture, pose, and emotional evocation (rasa).

Classical dances function as a form of total theater where the dancer acts out stories almost exclusively through gestures. Bharatanatyam from Tamil Nadu is a solo temple dance form characterized by earth-bound movements and rigorous physical training. Kathak, originating from northern storytellers (kathakas), emphasizes rhythmic foot movements adorned with small bells (ghungroo) and incorporates Persian influences from Mughal courts. Kathakali from Kerala is a highly stylized dance-drama featuring actors in elaborate makeup, colorful costumes, and face masks performing stories from Hindu epics. Kuchipudi from Andhra Pradesh combines pure dance and expressive sign language mime. Odissi from Odisha originates in Hindu temples and utilizes symbolic costumes and mudras. Manipuri features graceful, fluid upper body movements and the distinctive barrel-shaped Kumil skirt. Mohiniyattam from Kerala follows the gentle Lasya style, while Sattriya originated in the Vaishnavism monasteries of Assam.

Alongside classical traditions, India hosts a vast array of folk and tribal dances that remain vital in rural areas. These include Bhangra and Giddha in Punjab, Garba and Dandiya in Gujarat, Lavani in Maharashtra, and Bihu in Assam. Folk dances are primarily oral traditions passed down through generations, depicting daily life, social relationships, and seasonal rituals using locally made percussion instruments.

sections.origins_and_history: The origins of dance in India date back to paleolithic and neolithic cave paintings at Bhimbetka rock shelters. Archaeological evidence includes the 2500 BCE Dancing Girl figurine from the Indus Valley Civilisation. Vedic literature integrated rituals with dramatic performance, while early performance texts like the Natasutras date to around 500-600 BCE. The primary surviving treatise is the Natya Shastra, compiled between 200 BCE and 200 CE.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Classical Indian dance uses a codified system of gesture, mime, and facial expression (abhinaya and mudras) to enact stories. Dancers synchronize their repertoire with vocalists and an orchestra, utilizing rhythmic footwork adorned with ghungroo bells. Folk and tribal dances range from gentle, groovy movements to elevated, vigorous limb involvement reflecting daily village life and rituals.
sections.music_and_instruments: Classical dances are accompanied by Carnatic or Hindustani music, featuring vocalists and traditional orchestras. Folk and tribal dances rely on indigenous instruments, particularly percussion, producing aesthetics ranging from mild and soothing to strong, weighted rhythms.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances feature regional costumes and specific aesthetic markers, such as the elaborately painted faces and masks of Kathakali, the barrel-shaped Kumil skirt of Manipuri, and ghungroo ankle bells. Settings historically include Hindu temples, monastery halls (namghar), and royal courts, alongside modern stages.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dances serve as devotional and narrative art forms, enacting stories from Hindu epics like the Mahabharata and Ramayana, as well as myths of Krishna, Shiva, and Shakti. Group folk dances are performed during seasonal and religious festivals such as Durga Puja and Navaratri.

sections.lineage: Indian dancing traditions have influenced dance forms across South Asia and Southeast Asia.

profile.sacred_note: All classical dances of India have roots in Hindu arts and religious practices, often preceded by traditional cleansing and offering rituals such as rangapuja and purvaranga.

basic_steps: Rhythmic foot stamping adorned with ghungroo
teaching.rhythm: Set to tala and raga structures in classical Carnatic or Hindustani music
teaching.formation: Solo or team performances depending on the specific classical or folk style
teaching.level_notes: Requires extensive physical training, textual study, and synchronization with vocalists and orchestra.

music_profile.vocal_style: Classical vocalists delivering lines and songs in traditional languages like Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, and Malayalam
music_profile.sound_description: Music is produced through indigenous instruments and vocal accompaniment, ranging from mild and soothing to strong and weighted rhythms.

movement_profile.posture: Legs and torso generally straight in Kathak; erdbezogene earth-bound postures in Bharatanatyam
movement_profile.footwork: Rhythmic foot movements adorned with small bells (Ghungroo)
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Developed vocabulary based on gestures of arms and upper body movement, mudras
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Bends, turns, and graceful fluid upper body movements
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Stage movements, solo or group performances in temples, courts, or community halls
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Varies from slow sopana melody to vigorous limb involvement

signature_moves.name: Nataraja Tandava
signature_moves.description: Cosmic dance performed by the god Shiva

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Extensive training required; some tribal dances involve elevated and vigorous involvement of limbs

episode_brief.logline: Explore the ancient roots and vibrant regional diversity of Indian classical and folk dance traditions.
beats: View paleolithic cave paintings at Bhimbetka showing early dance scenes.
Examine the 2500 BCE Dancing Girl figurine from the Indus Valley Civilisation.
Explore the foundational text Natya Shastra and its classification of classical arts.
Witness a Bharatanatyam solo performance from Tamil Nadu.
Observe the elaborate makeup and martial arts movements of Kathakali in Kerala.
Experience the energetic folk rhythms of Bhangra in Punjab.

lesson_ladder.goal: Understand basic hand gestures and posture

drills: Practice rhythmic foot stamping with ghungroo
Perform abhinaya facial expressions for mythological stories
Combine pure dance (nritta) with expressive mime (nritya)

episode_brief.instructor_persona: A rigorous guru trained in traditional guru-shishya parampara, emphasizing textual history and precise physical execution.
episode_brief.music_cue: Traditional Carnatic vocal piece accompanied by percussion and ankle bells.
